title: 2026 ACA Marketplace Costs Rise as Enrollment Falls
description_short: KFF found 2026 Marketplace premiums and deductibles rose, while plan selections fell; Ohio and Oklahoma selections declined 20% and 15%.
description_medium: KFF found average ACA Marketplace premium payments rose from $113 per month in 2025 to $178 in 2026, while average deductibles increased 37% to $3,786. Open-enrollment plan selections fell by more than one million to 23.1 million; selections declined 20% in Ohio and 15% in Oklahoma. These are plan-selection figures, not February counts of people still covered.
description_long: After enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, KFF found that average monthly Marketplace premium payments rose from $113 to $178 in 2026, a 58% increase. Average deductibles increased 37% to $3,786. During 2026 open enrollment, plan selections fell by more than one million to 23.1 million; KFF reported declines of 20% in Ohio and 15% in Oklahoma. Those state figures measure plan selections, not the number of residents who remained insured in February. KFF separately projected that average effectuated enrollment could fall from 22.3 million in 2025 to about 17.5 million in 2026, possibly 16.5 million. A later Reuters report published September 25 described nearly three million people as having dropped ACA plans during 2026. That subsequent national report is a separate measure and does not substantiate the original February comparison or one-third state-loss claims. The corrected account distinguishes costs, sign-ups, enrollment projections, and later reported exits.

https://www.kff.org/affordable-care-act/: Average monthly ACA Marketplace premium payments rose from $113 in 2025 to $178 in 2026, a 58% increase; average deductibles rose 37% to $3,786.
2026 open-enrollment plan selections fell by over one million to 23.1 million; state selections fell 20% in Ohio and 15% in Oklahoma.
KFF projected average effectuated enrollment could fall from 22.3 million in 2025 to about 17.5 million in 2026, potentially 16.5 million.
https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation: Reuters reported nearly three million people had dropped ACA plans during 2026; this is later national reporting, not a February comparison or the KFF state plan-selection measure.

notes: Corrected the measure and geography: the state percentages are changes in 2026 plan selections, not February coverage losses.

title: Trump's 2025 Disclosure Lists Millions in Branded-Product Royalties
description_short: Trump's 2025 financial disclosure listed millions in royalties from branded watches, footwear, fragrances, the Greenwood Bible, and NFTs.
description_medium: Reuters reported that Trump's 2025 financial disclosure listed about $2.8 million in watch royalties, $2.5 million from sneakers and fragrances, $1.3 million from the Greenwood Bible, and $1.16 million from NFTs. The filing appears largely to cover 2024. It documents reported private-business income, not sales from the Oval Office or White House-operated businesses.
description_long: Reuters reported that Donald Trump's 2025 financial disclosure listed royalty and licensing income from Trump-branded products, including about $2.8 million from watches, $2.5 million from sneakers and fragrances, $1.3 million from the Greenwood Bible, and $1.16 million from NFTs. Reuters said the filing appeared largely to cover calendar year 2024, so these are reported income figures from a disclosure, not a tally of 2025 retail sales. The filing does not establish that the products were sold from the Oval Office, that the White House operated the businesses, or that presidential duties generated the income. It records private commercial interests while Trump held office, a fact distinct from evidence about how any particular sale was marketed. The disclosure and the Reuters reports cited here also do not support the original entry's claims about a $5 million Gold Card, 21 foreign real-estate projects, or nearly $1.2 billion in later-year income. Those claims require separate records and sources. This correction is limited to the merchandise and licensing amounts reported in the 2025 filing.

Reuters described the filing as appearing largely to cover 2024.

title: Trump Calls Musk's Proposed America Party “Ridiculous”
description_short: After Musk proposed an America Party amid a dispute over Trump's spending bill, Trump called the idea “ridiculous” on July 6, 2025.
description_medium: Trump and Elon Musk's dispute over the tax-and-spending bill resurfaced when Musk proposed an America Party in July 2025. On July 6, Trump called the proposal “ridiculous.” Reuters documented that exchange and related investor reaction. The cited reporting does not substantiate the stored nicknames, deepfake claims, or a continuous feud dominating July and August.
description_long: The public dispute between Donald Trump and Elon Musk over the administration's tax-and-spending bill resurfaced in July 2025. Reuters reported that Musk proposed an America Party after opposing the bill, and that Trump called the idea “ridiculous” on July 6. A separate Reuters report described an investment firm's decision to postpone a Tesla exchange-traded fund after Musk announced his political plan. Earlier in June, Trump blamed Musk's criticism on the bill's electric-vehicle tax-credit provisions, according to the Reuters report carried by Investing.com. These reports establish a public disagreement and specific responses; they do not establish every detail in the original account. The reviewed sources do not verify the quoted nicknames “Baby Elon” or “Low-IQ Elon,” nor the claim that Musk amplified deepfakes throughout July and August. The account is therefore dated to the documented July exchange and does not characterize the dispute as continuous or infer that the proposed party became an established political organization.

title: Ivanka Trump Brand Imports Rose an Estimated 166% in 2016
description_short: A 2017 report said U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise rose an estimated 166% in 2016; the figure measures imports, not sales.
description_medium: An Associated Press report published in April 2017 said U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise, almost all from China, rose an estimated 166% in 2016. It separately reported that the brand's sales reached record levels in 2017. The 166% figure is an import estimate based on shipping data, not sales growth or profit, and does not show that White House service caused the change.
description_long: An Associated Press report published by CBS News on April 18, 2017 said U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise had risen an estimated 166% in the prior year, with almost all of the goods coming from China. The report attributed the import estimate to Panjiva, which analyzes shipping records. It separately said the brand's sales reached record levels in 2017. These are different measures: imported merchandise records goods entering the country, while sales and profit describe commercial results. The 166% figure therefore cannot accurately be described as a 166% rise in brand sales, nor does the comparison by itself establish what caused the import increase. The reporting appeared as Ivanka Trump began a White House role and discussed scrutiny of her ongoing private business interests, but it did not prove that government service produced the commercial growth. The corrected title preserves the documented import statistic and removes the unsupported claim that sales surged by that amount during the first year of the presidency.

notes: Corrected the metric and date: the 166% statistic describes estimated 2016 imports; the report separately says 2017 sales reached record levels.

title: Trump Pardons Former Sheriff Joe Arpaio in August 2017
description_short: On August 25, 2017, Trump granted former Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio a full pardon for criminal contempt.
description_medium: On August 25, 2017, President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to former Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio, who had been convicted of criminal contempt for disobeying a federal court order in the Melendres case. The pardon occurred during Trump's first term, not on January 20, 2025, and was not a second-term clemency action.
description_long: On August 25, 2017, President Donald Trump granted former Maricopa County sheriff Joe Arpaio a full and unconditional pardon. Arpaio had been convicted of criminal contempt after disobeying a federal court order in the Melendres v. Arpaio case. The White House press release and the signed pardon warrant document the date and the clemency action. The pardon was issued during Trump's first term; it was not a January 20, 2025 action or a second-term policy decision. The correction preserves the legal scope of the event: a presidential pardon forgave Arpaio's federal criminal-contempt conviction, but the pardon did not itself erase the underlying court order or establish that the conduct leading to the conviction was lawful. The source record documents an individual act of clemency. It does not establish that the pardon formally created a later policing policy or served as an official model for second-term enforcement. Those broader interpretations should remain separate from the dated facts of the pardon and the conviction.

https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/document: The archived White House press release states Trump granted Arpaio a pardon on August 25, 2017 and identifies him as former Maricopa County sheriff.
https://www.justice.gov/pardon/file/9935: The Department of Justice pardon warrant records the signed clemency instrument and its full and unconditional scope.

notes: Replaced the erroneous second-term framing with the first-term pardon date; removed the unsupported claim that the pardon established a second-term policing model.

title: Trump's “Unpresidented” Tweet About China's Drone Seizure
description_short: On December 17, 2016, President-elect Trump misspelled “unprecedented” as “unpresidented” in a tweet about China's seizure of a U.S. Navy drone.
description_medium: On December 17, 2016, President-elect Donald Trump criticized China's seizure of a U.S. Navy underwater drone in a tweet that misspelled “unprecedented” as “unpresidented.” He deleted the post about an hour later and replaced it with corrected wording. Contemporary coverage documented the typo and the public reaction; the original December 30 date is wrong.
description_long: On December 17, 2016, President-elect Donald Trump posted a tweet criticizing China's seizure of a U.S. Navy research drone in international waters. He called the seizure an “unpresidented” act, misspelling “unprecedented.” Contemporary reports said the tweet was deleted about an hour later and replaced with a version using the correct spelling. The typo quickly drew online mockery and became the focus of news coverage. The event should be dated to December 17, when the post appeared, rather than December 30 as in the original entry. The source reports establish the wording, the subject of the tweet, and the deletion and correction. They do not show that the spelling error changed U.S. policy, caused a diplomatic outcome, or reflected a particular review process. The documented episode is a corrected social-media post about a real international incident, not evidence by itself of broader claims about literacy or the consequences of social-media diplomacy.

notes: Corrected the date to the publication date of the tweet and limited significance claims to what the contemporary reports document.

title: Vance Criticizes European Governments at Munich Security Conference
description_short: At the Munich Security Conference on February 14, 2025, JD Vance criticized European governments over speech, migration, and democratic practices.
description_medium: At the Munich Security Conference on February 14, 2025, Vice President JD Vance criticized European governments over speech restrictions, migration, and what he described as democratic backsliding. Reuters reported public pushback from European officials. The cited coverage does not support the claim that Vance called leaders “freeloaders” or that NATO officials privately equated his rhetoric with Kremlin messaging.
description_long: Vice President JD Vance used his February 14, 2025, speech at the Munich Security Conference to criticize European governments. Reuters reported that he focused on freedom of speech, migration, and what he characterized as democratic backsliding, arguing that European leaders were restricting political debate and excluding voters. European officials publicly challenged parts of his account, making the speech a source of diplomatic friction at a major transatlantic security meeting. The documented dispute was about Vance's criticism of European policy and the response it drew. The cited report does not substantiate the stored quotation that he repeatedly called European leaders “freeloaders,” nor does it establish that NATO officials privately described his remarks as indistinguishable from Kremlin messaging. It also does not prove that the speech caused lasting damage to the alliance. The corrected entry records the dated speech and reported public reaction without converting unverified quotations or private assessments into fact.

https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/van: Reuters reported Vance's February 14 Munich speech criticizing European governments on speech restrictions, migration, and democratic practice, along with public responses from European officials.

notes: Kept the supported speech and public reaction; removed the unverified “freeloaders” quotation and private NATO comparison.

title: Trump Administration Announces Review of About $9 Billion in Harvard Funding
description_short: On March 31, 2025, the administration announced a review of about $9 billion in Harvard federal grants and contracts, citing antisemitism allegations.
description_medium: On March 31, 2025, the Trump administration announced a review of roughly $9 billion in federal grants and contracts to Harvard, citing allegations of antisemitism. The reported amount was funding under review, not money canceled that day. This was a March review; broader policy demands and a funding freeze were later developments, not a February threat combined with the review.
description_long: On March 31, 2025, the Trump administration announced that it would review roughly $9 billion in federal grants and contracts to Harvard, citing allegations of antisemitism. The figure described the value of funding under review; the announcement did not say that $9 billion had already been canceled. The date and scope correct the original entry, which described a February letter and combined the review with a list of university-governance demands. Those are not established by the cited March 31 report. Broader demands and a funding freeze were later developments, but they are separate actions and should not be collapsed into the March review or assigned the same date. The available source does not identify which individual grants or contracts were affected, what amount was ultimately canceled, or the outcome of each funding decision. The supported event is the dated announcement of a review, its approximate funding scope, and the administration's stated rationale—not a completed $9 billion cut or a February ultimatum.

https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-revi: Reuters reported the March 31, 2025 announcement to review roughly $9 billion in Harvard grants and federal contracts, citing antisemitism allegations.

notes: Kept the March 31 review distinct from later demands and freezes; no grant-level or final cancellation claims are made.

title: Trump Signs Order Enforcing Hyde Amendment Restrictions on Federal Abortion Funding
description_short: On January 24, 2025, Trump ordered agencies to enforce Hyde Amendment restrictions and revoked two Biden reproductive-health executive orders.
description_medium: On January 24, 2025, Trump signed an order directing agencies to enforce the Hyde Amendment and revoking two Biden abortion-access executive orders. OMB's later implementation guidance retained legally authorized exceptions for rape, incest, and life-saving care. The order did not eliminate those statutory exceptions or establish specific later denials of care.
description_long: On January 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order directing federal agencies to enforce the Hyde Amendment and revoking Executive Orders 14076 and 14079, which had directed agencies to promote reproductive-health access. The White House order set a federal funding policy and instructed the Office of Management and Budget to issue implementation guidance. In a later memorandum, OMB described how agencies should apply the policy and retained exceptions when federal law authorizes payment for care involving rape, incest, or life-saving treatment, subject to applicable law. The order's signing date is January 24, not January 20. It did not eliminate those exceptions, as the original synopsis claimed. The order and memorandum document federal directives; they do not, by themselves, establish that a named patient was denied care or that access changed in a particular federal program. Those consequences require separate evidence. This account separates the executive order from the later implementation memo and states their scope without claiming specific patient outcomes.

title: State Department Expands Online Vetting for Student and Exchange Visitor Visas
description_short: In June 2025, the State Department expanded online-presence screening for F, M, and J visa applicants; social-media identifiers were already collected under a 2019 policy.
description_medium: The State Department began requesting social-media identifiers from most U.S. visa applicants worldwide in 2019. In June 2025, it directed more comprehensive online-presence screening for F, M, and J student and exchange-visitor visa applicants as appointments resumed, and asked applicants to make profiles public. These distinct policies do not support the original claim of a January 20 order covering every applicant.
description_long: The 2025 student-visa screening directive was not the start of social-media collection for all U.S. visa applicants. The State Department said it began requesting social-media identifiers from most immigrant and nonimmigrant applicants worldwide in 2019, including identifiers used during the preceding five years. In June 2025, as student and exchange-visitor appointments resumed, the department directed more comprehensive online-presence review for applicants in the F, M, and J visa categories and asked them to make social-media profiles public for review. The measures have different dates and scopes: the older policy requested identifiers from most visa applicants, while the 2025 directive added screening for specified student and exchange-visitor categories. The cited sources do not support a January 20, 2025 executive order requiring every applicant to provide five years of social-media history, nor do they establish that applicants were denied visas for protected political expression or that the policy primarily targeted people from Muslim-majority countries. Those claims should not be presented as fact without additional evidence.

https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/: The State Department's 2019 notice says it began requesting social-media identifiers from most immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants worldwide, covering identifiers used in the preceding five years.
